conventions: The chapter's three lə-X lə-Y possessive phrases — לְכִסֵּא־לָךְ (v11, v12) and לְמוֹשָׁב לוֹ (v13) — are read alike: the first לְ takes the preposition the ASV writes (upon, for), the second לְ is its own unrepresented unit under rule 40 because the ASV recasts it as a possessive determiner on the noun standing beside it, and that suffix takes the determiner (thy, his). BSB's contrary treatment at v12 is the documented convention difference and not an error.

The supplied with of clothe X with Y (v9, v16, v18) and satisfy X with Y (v15) renders a Hebrew double accusative: the second noun is the verb's own object, so the preposition the English verb needs to reach it joins the verb's unit under rule 44 and the noun keeps only its own word. אֱמֶת in v11 is the counter-case: an adverbial accusative of manner, whose supplied in is the noun's under rule 33. Run the direct-object question first; the availability of another English preposition decides nothing here.

The only added units in the chapter are the And of v2 and the Or of v4, each a coordinator the ASV writes at the head of a colon the Hebrew juxtaposes with no conjunction in it at all (rule 14). Every other connective answers to a written morpheme, including the postposed also of v16 (rule 51) and the Nor of v3, which is the second oath אִם. That אִם of vv. 3–4 is the negative oath particle throughout and takes whatever negative the ASV writes for it — Surely ... not (v3, discontinuous under rule 25), Nor (v3), not (v4); it is never unrepresented and the negation is never handed to the verb.

Both construct chains fused into a single English word under rule 30 are headed by rule 23, but on opposite sides, and the test is which lexemes the English word writes. הֲדֹם רַגְלָיו → footstool (v7) is a compound writing both lexemes, so no morpheme is uniquely defensible and the head goes to the governing morpheme, the construct הֲדֹם. עֶרֶשׂ יְצוּעָי → bed (v3) writes one lexeme, and the ASV's own literal margin distributes couch to עֶרֶשׂ and bed to יְצוּעַי, corroborating without deciding under rule 38, so the head goes to יָצוּעַ. The competing head on the construct עֶרֶשׂ remains defensible, both lemmas being ordinary ASV bed words; it is recorded here because the v3 note names only the competing unrepresented reading.

יְרַנֵּנוּ is rendered shout for joy in both v9 and v16 and heads on shout as the lexical predicate; the competing head on joy under rule 44's light-verb clause is named in both notes. The two verses are the chapter's own subtraction test for rule 56: they render the same verb identically and differ only by the aloud of v16, which is what the infinitive absolute רַנֵּן standing there is rendered by, as בָּרֵךְ takes abundantly in v15.
report: Checked all 22 candidate lemma groups and read the whole dump end to end for the splits the lemma table cannot see (added units, head choices, fused pairs). No real split found; every difference is licensed by the source or by what the ASV actually wrote. No patches.

לְ, the largest group, differs only by construction: dative after a verb of swearing (v2, v11 unto), benefactive (v1, v5, v13, v17 for), goal (v3, v7, v8 into; v7 at), the throne relation (v11, v12 upon), and the recast genitive of v17 of. The three lə-X lə-Y phrases — לְכִסֵּא־לָךְ in v11 and v12, לְמוֹשָׁב לוֹ in v13 — are read identically: the first לְ takes the written preposition, the second is unrepresented under rule 40, and its suffix takes the possessive determiner the recasting writes.

אִם in v3 (twice) and v4 is one construction read one way: the negative oath particle takes whatever negative the ASV wrote for it — Surely ... not, Nor, not. The Nor of v3 rests on a particle that is present; the Or of v4 opens a colon with no conjunction in it at all and is added, as is the And of v2. Those two are the chapter's only added units, and nowhere else is a supplied connective folded into a neighbouring morpheme.

The two rule-30 fusions of construct chains head on opposite morphemes — הֲדֹם רַגְלָיו → footstool on the construct (v7), עֶרֶשׂ יְצוּעָי → bed on the rectum (v3). That is the two branches of rule 23 and not a split: footstool is a compound writing both lexemes, so the tie-break heads on the governing morpheme, while bed writes one lexeme, and the ASV's own literal margin (Hebrew the couch of my bed) puts bed on יְצוּעַי and couch on עֶרֶשׂ, corroborating without deciding under rule 38. The competing head on עֶרֶשׂ is defensible and is now named in the convention log, since the v3 note names only the competing unrepresented reading.

The supplied with of v9, v15, v16 and v18 is consistent: in each the noun after it is the verb's own accusative object (Hebrew double accusative), so rule 44 puts the word in the verb's unit. v11's אֱמֶת is the counter-case rather than a competing treatment — an adverbial accusative of manner, whose supplied in belongs to the noun under rule 33. The direct-object question, not the availability of another preposition, is what separates them.

רָנַן heads on shout in both v9 and v16, each note naming the competing head on joy; the two verses are a clean minimal pair for rule 56, since they render the same יְרַנֵּנוּ identically and differ only by the aloud that answers to v16's infinitive absolute רַנֵּן.

All four BSB disagreements are documented convention differences, not errors: אֵת at v1 (rule 16, the ASV writes the object bare), the paragogic he at v8 (rule 32, BSB attaches it to its host), the second לְ of v12 (rule 40, BSB attaches the preposition to its phrase; the identical לְ at v11 was simply not flagged), and בְּ at v13 (rule 40, the ASV promotes Zion to a bare direct object). No edge was changed to improve the rate.

No promotion. Everything this chapter exercised is already written: rule 14's closing sentences for the supplied coordinators, rule 23's amendment for the fusion heads, rule 40 for the recast dative, rule 44 for the double-accusative with, rule 56 for both infinitives absolute. Five conventions recorded for judgments the repeated verse notes carried but the log did not.
